title: Thirty-nine minutes of AUsome.
summary: A 39-minute Massachusetts RMV wait becomes a dance party. A mother remembers a security guard, her son James, and connection with very few words.
search: A reflection & photo essayThirty-nine minutes of AUsome.A security guard, my son, and a dance party at the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles.An AUsome Life · A remembered moment at the Massachusetts RMV 01The RMV, of all places. One of my favorite memories of James happened at the Massachusetts RMV.We waited 39 minutes. And for that entire wait, a security guard kept my son company, entertained him, and showed him the kind of warmth that stays with a mother long after an errand is over.There was an impromptu dance party. Right there. At the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles.The usual seriousness of the place could wait.I can’t remember whether there was actual music. Some RMV Muzak drifting through the room, maybe. A cell phone playing somewhere. Or perhaps they were dancing to some shared, unspoken groove.And does it even matter?I remember the two of them. Whatever the music was, or wasn’t, they had found each other. 02An arm lifted. An answer. 03The conversation keeps going. I love looking at these photographs. James in his red shorts and blue shoes. The guard in his uniform, his badge still hanging at his waist. The tiled floor. The waiting-room chairs. The signs telling everybody where to go and what to have ready.And in the middle of all that ordinary, official business: these two.An arm goes up. Another follows. They turn toward each other. The next movement becomes another invitation, another response. James is right there in the exchange, bringing his own movement and attention to it.Few words passed between them. Yet watching them, I felt that everything that mattered in that moment was being communicated. There was a whole conversation happening on that tiled floor. 04Two people making something together. 05A waiting room with room for joy. The world isn’t always this AUsome. I wish it were.A family can love its life deeply and still need the world to do better by it. I know both of those feelings. I can treasure this memory and still wish that being welcomed so wholeheartedly felt more ordinary.In a life shaped in part by profound autism, so much thought goes into helping other people understand what James needs. Then someone comes along who takes an interest in him, finds a way to connect, and keeps showing up in that connection. For the length of a wait. For the length of a dance.Those people become part of our family’s story.This man gave James his attention throughout those 39 minutes. There was affection in it. Playfulness. A willingness to be a little silly in a room where people generally have other things on their minds. And James had something to give him, too. The photographs hold their back-and-forth. 06The warmth I remember. 07An ordinary errand. One of my favorite memories. Less than a week after this outing, James began having seizures. They are now under control with the care of the wonderful team at Mass General, and I am deeply grateful. That timing gives these photographs another layer of meaning for me. I come back to James’s part in all of this: his attention, his movement, the way he answered a gesture with one of his own. He and the guard made those 39 minutes together. I’m grateful I got to watch, and that these photographs let me revisit it. The people we meet are among the most profoundly AUsome parts of this life. Some stay. Some share a small stretch of it with us, and we carry that stretch for years.I hope this guard knows how much those minutes meant. I hope he knows that, somewhere, a mother still looks at these photographs and remembers how warmly he welcomed her son.There are so many things I want for James as he moves through the world. Friendship. Affection. The freedom to enjoy himself. People who notice what he is offering and respond.I got to watch that happen at the RMV.Thirty-nine minutes. Very few words. One of my favorite memories ever. The world isn’t always this AUsome. But when it is, it really is. title: I thought we were on opposite sides
summary: A mother's thank-you to her son's special education director, plus a plain-language guide to one-on-one aides, LRE and questions for your next IEP meeting.
search: PARENTING & ADVOCACYI thought we were on opposite sidesA beach moment brought me back to a disagreement over James’s one-on-one aide—and to gratitude for Roseanne B. With a parent guide to least restrictive environment.An AUsome Life · October 26, 2026 James at the beach. October 2026. Watching James at the beach yesterday, I wished Roseanne B. could see him. He was moving across the sand, safely, without an adult right at his side. I was there, watching—and feeling profoundly grateful to the special education director I once thought I was at war with. Roseanne had decades of experience. She would come to mean a great deal to me. But when I asked for James to have a one-on-one aide, we disagreed. I believed he needed someone specifically assigned to him. James has substantial support needs, and I wanted to be sure someone would notice when he needed help. Having an adult beside him seemed like the clearest way to make that happen. She declined. She explained her concern that, for James, the arrangement I was requesting could be more restrictive than he needed. At the time, that was hard to take in. I was asking for more help. How could that limit him? Many parents will recognize the feeling. You know school districts have finite resources, and you know your child's needs do not conveniently fit within them. It can be difficult to hear a refusal without feeling that you need to push harder. I was trying to protect my son. I still am. The principle behind our disagreement Roseanne was referring to least restrictive environment, or LRE, a requirement under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA). In plain language, schools must educate children with disabilities alongside children without disabilities to the maximum extent appropriate. Before moving a child into a separate setting, the team must consider whether education in a general education classroom can work satisfactorily with supplementary aids and services.1 That support is part of the requirement. It can enable a child to participate in classrooms, extracurricular activities, and other parts of school life.2 A one-on-one aide is not automatically a more restrictive placement. For some children, an aide makes inclusion possible. Decisions about support must be grounded in the individual child's needs.13 What I appreciate now is the care that question deserved: how could James receive the help he needed while also having opportunities to initiate, make choices, and use his developing skills? I understand better why Roseanne wanted us to consider how the support would work in practice. Looking back, I am grateful for the experience she brought to that conversation. Watching him move across the sand brought that earlier conversation back to me. What stayed with me yesterday At the beach, I was thinking about James and the space around him. About being there, paying attention, while he moved without someone immediately beside him. School placement law does not tell a parent how far away to stand on a beach. But the question Roseanne helped me consider has stayed with me beyond school: where does James need our help, and where can we give him room? That answer changes with the situation. Yesterday, I could see what that room meant. I wanted him to have the support he needed. I wanted him to have this freedom, too. I thought of Roseanne, and of the whole village around James: the teachers, aides, therapists, and family members who have helped him learn and grow. So many people contribute to a child's life through patient, everyday care. And there was James, using his skills. Moving across the sand. Enjoying his day. I was proud of him, and grateful for the people who have supported him along the way. The people who help our children grow do not always get to see the moments their care has helped make possible. A school conversation can stay with a parent long after the meeting ends. Yesterday, on a beach, I felt a deeper appreciation for one of ours. It takes a village. Sometimes you feel the work of that village in a moment when your child has a little more room around him, and you can watch what he does with it. I once thought Roseanne and I were on opposite sides. Yesterday, I wished she could see James enjoying that space, and know how grateful I am for what she helped me understand. Roseanne, I thought of you yesterday. Thank you for being part of our village. Someone in your village came to mind? Send them this story with a thank-you of your own.A PARENT'S GUIDEOne-on-one aides and LRE: a parent's guideWhat U.S. special education law protects, why it matters, and five questions to take to your next IEP meeting. Open the sections that are useful to you. What does the law protect—and why does it matter?IDEA gives eligible children a right to a free appropriate public education, commonly called FAPE. Its LRE provisions protect their opportunity to learn alongside peers without disabilities, with appropriate support, rather than being separated by default.14A child's placement must be based on their IEP and determined by a group that includes parents and people knowledgeable about the child, evaluation information, and placement options. The team must also consider possible harmful effects on the child or the quality of services.3The goal is an appropriate education with meaningful opportunities to participate. Being physically present in a classroom does not, by itself, explain whether a child's educational needs are being met. Does least restrictive mean fewer services?No. Supplementary aids and services are part of IDEA's approach to inclusion. They can support participation in regular classes and other school activities.2For some children, individual adult assistance helps them access instruction, communication, personal care, or activities. An aide is a support, not automatically a separate educational placement. The team needs to consider what the child requires and how the assistance will be provided.15A practical concern about excessive prompting or adult proximity should be examined in the child's actual circumstances. It is not a blanket reason to withhold needed help. Five questions for your next IEP meetingStart with the need. Which parts of the day are difficult? What observations or assessments show where support is required?Ask for specifics. If the team says an aide would be more restrictive, which opportunities might be limited, and what evidence supports that concern for your child?Examine the proposed alternative. Who will provide help, when will they be available, and what happens if they are absent?Include your child's communication. Consider preferences expressed through speech, AAC, gestures, expressions, and other communication.Plan how to review it. What information will show whether the arrangement is working? When will the team meet again?These are discussion prompts. The IEP itself must specify services and supports, anticipated frequency, location and duration, and how progress toward annual goals will be measured.5 What if the district says no—or cites limited resources?Ask for the educational reasons and the information behind the decision. Expertise matters, and parents deserve an explanation grounded in their child's needs.When a district refuses a requested change concerning identification, evaluation, placement, or provision of FAPE, IDEA requires prior written notice. It must explain the refusal, the assessments or records used, and the other options considered and rejected.6Staffing or resource shortages do not erase a district's obligation to provide FAPE in the least restrictive environment.7My gratitude in this story reflects our family's experience. Parents who disagree with a decision can seek information and support through their state's parent training center, an advocate, or a qualified special education attorney. Where can families find help?Across the United States: the Center for Parent Information and Resources directory helps families find Parent Training and Information Centers and Community Parent Resource Centers in their state or territory.9In Massachusetts: Massachusetts DESE's Families & Guardians page links to the state parent guide, procedural safeguards, information about selecting an advocate, and family organizations.The Federation for Children with Special Needs is another starting point for family information and support.8 A question to bring with you: “How will this plan meet my child's needs while supporting participation, choice, and opportunities to develop skills—and how will we know whether it is working?” Law and parent resources 34 CFR § 300.114 — Least restrictive environment requirements. 34 CFR § 300.42 — Supplementary aids and services. 34 CFR § 300.116 — Individualized placement decisions and parent involvement. title: Wicked Whoopies: a little stop with a very large whoopie pie.
summary: A family visit to Wicked Whoopies in Freeport, Maine: James, giant whoopie-pie displays, a colorful shop and useful sensory and access planning notes.
search: Freeport, Maine · From the family album Wicked Whoopies: a little stop with a very large whoopie pie. Orange walls, turquoise chairs, and a stack of whoopie pies taller than James. A Maine treat stop with a sense of humor. October 16, 2026 · A family visit The full-size James and the considerably oversized whoopie pies. From our family camera roll. A shop with a tower of whoopie pies has made its intentions quite clear. We are here for something sweet, and nobody is taking the décor too seriously. Our visit to Wicked Whoopies in Freeport, Maine, gave us exactly the sort of photographs I love keeping: James in his pink shirt, a wrapped treat in hand, standing beside a display that is delightfully out of proportion. The room is full of color. Orange walls, purple shelving, turquoise tables and chairs, blue flowers, and enormous red letters spelling “SMILE.” It is cheerful, a little theatrical, and thoroughly committed to its subject. A whoopie pie apparently deserves a pedestal. Several, in fact. James wore his hearing protection, as you can see in the photographs. That belongs in the family album just as much as the treat and the pink shirt. The pictures also give another family a useful preview of the bright interior before deciding whether it looks like their kind of stop. Plenty of color, right down to the shelving. This wider view is useful if you like to see a place before arriving. What makes this worth considering is its scale as an outing. You can build a small plan around a treat shop without needing a whole afternoon of activities. A browse, a choice, a photograph if everyone wants one, and then on with the day. My favorite detail is the contrast between the whoopie pie in James’s hand and the enormous versions behind him. One for the road; several that would require a moving van. Keep the plan small. Show the shop photographs beforehand if a preview helps. Bring the hearing protection or communication supports your family usually uses. If a particular flavor matters, call before making the trip: the shop’s selection can differ from the online store. There were tables and chairs in the shop when these photos were taken. You can ask about seating when you call, or plan to take your purchase with you. A short visit is a perfectly reasonable plan. A smaller stack, and another picture worth keeping. The useful details. Sound and light: Expect a visually busy setting: saturated colors, oversized displays and bright overhead lighting. The photographs cannot tell us how loud the shop will be during your visit. Ask the shop about quieter times if that would help. Mobility and facilities: Our photos show indoor seating and the shop floor, but do not establish step-free entry, doorway clearance, accessible parking or restroom facilities. title: A camping swing, very much at home.
summary: Our portable Walmart swing, Yankee frugality, and autism-and-camping planning: familiar comforts, communication and room for a shorter trip. Original family photo.
search: Portable for camping · A little Yankee frugalityA camping swing, very much at home.Made for the campsite. Claimed by the stuffed animals. Our portable Walmart camping swing has earned its place at home, too—with a few thoughts on autism, camping, and bringing familiar comforts along.October 21, 2026 · From the family notebookOur Walmart camping swing, already full of stuffed animals, just after we moved in. Excuse the older photograph from just after we moved in, but this is one of those finds worth showing before the room is ready for its close-up. We love this swing. The stuffed animals seem fairly committed to it, too. It came from Walmart, and it was made for camping: an Ozark Trail hammock-style chair with its own folding frame. Not an elaborate installation. Not something that needed a dedicated room. Just a portable chair that turned out to be a very welcome part of our home. A little Yankee frugality. Yes, from Walmart.Our version of Yankee frugality is not about making life smaller. It is about getting good use out of what we bring into it. Does it work? Will we actually use it? Do we already own something that does the job?Something does not become less useful because it came from Walmart, or more useful because it came from a specialty catalog. A good find is a good find. We can appreciate a lovely old quilt and a practical camping chair in the same room. Neither needs to apologize for the other.Nor is thrift simply a contest to pay the least. The bargain that sits unused is not much of a bargain. A chair made for camping that also becomes a favorite at home has a rather better argument for its place.That is the appeal here: not buying a whole new room, not replacing something because it is no longer new, and not confusing an impressive label with a useful object. Just noticing what works for your family and continuing to enjoy it. The price tag is not the point. The life you get out of a thing is. Find it at Walmart.Check the blue Ozark Trail hammock-chair listing ↗Availability note, October 21, 2026: The blue listing showed shipping, pickup and delivery unavailable when checked. It remains useful for identifying the chair and reading reviews, but it is not a promise that you can order it today.Browse Walmart’s current hammock-chair listings ↗. Other designs are not the chair in our photograph and have not been tested by our family.These are ordinary, non-affiliate shopping links. Our photograph shows an earlier purchase, not a guarantee of an identical production version. Compare the exact model, seller, instructions, price and availability before ordering. The portable part is the point.This is camping furniture, and that is part of its appeal. Walmart’s description for this model lists a folding frame and an included carry bag for transport and storage. The chair can come along with the camping gear instead of being a permanent fixture.That is worth knowing whether your interest is campsite seating or a chair you can put away when you need the space. Our own photograph and firsthand story are from home; this is not a campsite field test.Other owners have plenty to say, too. On October 21, 2026, Walmart’s listing showed 4.3 out of 5 stars from 466 ratings. Positive reviews describe easy setup and comfort; not every owner agrees about the fit. Read the critical reviews as well as the enthusiastic ones. That is the retailer’s listing score, not our own testing score, and it can change. A favorite does not need a specialty label.At our house, the cozy, swing-style seat found a place among James’s favorite stuffed animals. We pay attention to what he actually enjoys, not only what a product label says it is supposed to do.Sometimes the useful things are specialized. Sometimes they are in the camping aisle. We are glad we found this one. A seat full of stuffed animals is not a showroom photograph, but it is a fairly good picture of something having found its place. Autism and camping: bring a little familiar with you. A change of scenery does not have to mean changing every familiar thing. That is the camping connection this chair makes us think about: a comfortable place someone already enjoys might be something to bring along, when it suits both the person and the setting. Start with the autistic person, not an “autism-friendly” shopping list. A child, teenager or adult might enjoy a moving seat, prefer a firm, still chair, or choose something else entirely. Their preferences come first. Our chair is a home favorite; the suggestions here are for planning, not an account of taking it camping. Try the smaller version. Explore the equipment at home, or consider a short outdoor visit before committing to an overnight. Sitting outside together can be the whole plan. Nobody has to graduate to a tent. Preview the everyday details. Look at campsite photographs and maps together. Ask about bathrooms, paths, lighting, neighboring sites and noise. Plan around the person’s actual access and sensory needs, rather than assuming outdoors always means quiet. Bring what already works. Familiar food, bedding or a preferred comfort item may be worth the packing space. Keep the person’s usual communication available, including AAC—augmentative and alternative communication—where used. Plan charging, weather protection and a familiar backup; a “screen-free” trip must not mean losing a way to communicate. Keep choices real. Leave time for pauses and a quieter place to go. Respect “no,” “break” and “all done,” however they are communicated. A shorter visit or going home is an option, not a failed outing. For a person who needs substantial support, include personal care, overnight support and an individual safety plan in the arrangements. Plan for water, roads, fire, weather and emergencies; do not assume mobile service will be available. A familiar chair cannot replace those supports. And there is our Yankee-frugality point again: begin with the person’s familiar things, not a new cartful of “sensory camping essentials.” Planning references, checked October 21, 2026: National Autistic Society: holiday planning for autistic people and families, and National Park Service: before a camping trip. These are general planning resources, not endorsements of this chair. For something you can adapt to your own day, try our visual visit planner or AAC-friendly outing note. A few details before you settle in.Check the instructions, assembly, weight limit and intended movement for the exact chair you buy. Use a level, clear space and keep loose cords away from the frame and entry path; our moving-in photograph is a family snapshot, not a recommended setup. A camping chair is not automatically a therapeutic swing or suitable for every person. Follow the manufacturer’s guidance and provide the support or supervision the person needs.Product sources checked October 21, 2026: Walmart’s blue chair listing and customer ratings, and Walmart Business’s description of the same model for its folding frame and carry bag.
